text: George Harrison's song Something appears on Abbey Road.
note: Attached straight 's marks possession of the whole name, so it stays outside. Local experiment 265 got 'George'.

text: George Harrison’s guitar was a Rickenbacker.
note: Curly ’s stays outside, as straight 's does.

text: Octopus's Garden was Ringo Starr's song.
note: Middle 's belongs to the title and stays inside. Trailing 's stays outside.

text: Fans loved the Beatles' album.
note: Bare ' after plural s is a possessive and stays outside. Lowercase 'the' stays outside.

text: Fans loved the Beatles’ album.
note: Curly bare ’ after s, same rule.

text: Students read John Keats' poems in class.
note: Bare ' after a singular name ending in s.

text: Charles Dickens's novel Bleak House is long.
note: s's form. The whole 's stays outside.

text: Sinead O'Brien's bakery opened in Galway.
note: The apostrophe in O'Brien is part of the name. The trailing 's is not.

text: The band covered Rock 'n' Roll Music at the show.
note: Apostrophes inside a title stay inside.

text: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band came out in 1967.
note: Title starts with an abbreviation and holds a middle 's.

text: We met outside McDonald's in Leeds.
note: The 's is part of the company's own name, so it stays inside. A plain trailing-'s trim gets this wrong; a keep-list entry fixes it.

text: McDonald's menu changed, and Sainsbury's prices rose.
note: A name that ends in 's, used as a possessive. The name keeps its own 's; no second 's is written.

text: Tolkien's The Hobbit sold millions.
note: Possessive name directly before a title. Also names side by side.

text: NASA's rover reached Mars.
note: Possessive on an all-caps short form.

text: The prize went to Maria's team.
note: Single-word possessive name.

text: Beyoncé’s album Lemonade topped the charts.
note: Curly ’s after an accented letter.

text: On Revolver Paul McCartney sang Eleanor Rigby.
note: Two names of different kinds touch. Local experiment 265 merged them.

text: In Liverpool John Lennon met Paul McCartney.
note: Place then person with no word between.

text: At Abbey Road Studios George Martin recorded Revolver.
note: Local experiment 265 lost both names.

text: The producer told Paul John had left.
note: Two people side by side, same kind. In/out tagging cannot separate them even with kinds.

text: For Microsoft Satya Nadella spoke first.
note: Organisation then person.

text: She flew into Portland Oregon last spring.
note: Two places, same kind, no comma. Universal NER tags adjacent places separately.

text: In 1969 Apple Records released Abbey Road.
note: A year before a name is not a name.

text: Ringo Starr sang "Octopus's Garden" on Abbey Road.
note: Quote marks stay outside. Local experiment 265 kept them.

text: John Lennon wrote "Help!" for the film.
note: The ! belongs to the title. The quotes do not.

text: Ringo Starr sang 'Boys' on stage.
note: Single straight quotes. The closing ' after s is a quote, not a possessive.

text: Critics called the record “The White Album” for years.
note: Curly double quotes. Capital The inside a title stays inside.

text: Her favourite song is ‘Blackbird’.
note: Curly single quotes, then a sentence period.

text: "Imagine" was written by John Lennon.
note: Quoted title at the very start.

text: The title “Don’t Pass Me By” was Ringo’s first.
note: Curly apostrophe inside a quoted title stays; curly ’s on Ringo stays outside.

text: He joined Oxfam (the charity) in 2010.
note: A bracket after a name is outside.

text: The novel (Middlemarch) runs to 800 pages.
note: Name wrapped in round brackets.

text: The committee [of the United Nations] met.
note: Square bracket closes right after the name.

text: Did you hear Help!, the song?
note: Title ! stays, the comma after it goes. Local experiment 265 got this right.

text: Have you been to Rome?
note: Sentence ? stays outside.

text: She works at Yahoo! in London.
note: The ! is part of the company name.

text: The band Panic! at the Disco played Chicago.
note: Internal ! and lowercase words inside a band name.

text: They visited Washington, D.C., in May.
note: Internal comma and final period belong to the name. The second comma does not.

text: We met at St. Mary's Church; it was cold.
note: Abbreviation period and middle 's inside; semicolon outside.

text: Is Brazil bigger than Peru?
note: Question mark after the last name.

text: Ali said: Kenya is home.
note: Colon after a name.

text: The company is Acme Widgets Inc.
note: One period ends both the abbreviation and the sentence. The name keeps it.

text: Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds is on Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band.
note: Lowercase words inside titles; sentence period outside.

text: She opened an account at Bank of America.
note: Lowercase 'of' inside an organisation name.

text: The Lord of the Rings was filmed in New Zealand.
note: Capital The starts the title and stays inside.

text: Gone with the Wind won in 1940.
note: Title at the start with lowercase words.

text: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.
note: Lowercase particle inside a person's name; lowercase 'the' before a title stays outside.

text: Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn.
note: Lowercase 'van' inside a person's name.

text: Hewlett-Packard and Coca-Cola sponsored the event.
note: Hyphens inside names stay.

text: The London-based firm hired Jean-Paul Sartre's nephew.
note: Only London is the name in London-based. Universal NER would include '-based'. Whitespace splitting cannot return London alone.

text: The Paris–Rome train was late.
note: En dash joins two places with no space.

text: Mary Robinson-Smith joined Rolls-Royce.
note: Hyphenated surname and company.

text: He writes an anti-Microsoft blog.
note: A name inside a hyphenated word.

text: J.R.R. Tolkien wrote The Hobbit.
note: Initials with periods inside a name.

text: She moved to the U.S. last year.
note: Short form with a final period mid-sentence.

text: He moved to the U.S.
note: One period ends both the short form and the sentence. The name keeps it.

text: The BBC interviewed Dr. Jane Goodall.
note: A title such as Dr. stays outside a person's name.

text: Martin Luther King Jr. spoke in Washington.
note: Jr. with its period is part of the name.

text: The U.N. met in Geneva.
note: Short form for an organisation.

text: E. M. Forster wrote A Passage to India.
note: Spaced initials; title starts with capital A.

text: FANS SAW PAUL MCCARTNEY IN HAMBURG.
note: All caps. Capital letters give no clue.

text: i saw paul mccartney in liverpool yesterday.
note: All lower case. Universal NER counts case variants as names.

text: we bought an iphone from apple.
note: Lowercase product and company.

text: eBay sold the iPod.
note: Names that start lower case.

text: He loves Apple pie and Apple phones.
note: The first Apple is ordinary food; the second names the company.

text: The swift bird flew past Taylor Swift.
note: A common word that is also a surname (WNUT-17 reports this confusion).

text: She studied at the University of Liverpool.
note: One whole name. Liverpool is not tagged on its own.

text: The Bank of England raised rates.
note: Whole name only.

text: He works at New York University in Manhattan.
note: A place inside an organisation name is not tagged.

text: The Duke of Wellington won at Waterloo.
note: A title-name for a person; lowercase 'the' outside.

text: The Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra played in Leeds.
note: Place word starts an organisation name.

text: John, Paul, George and Ringo walked across Abbey Road.
note: Four people in a list. Abbey Road is the street here, so place.

text: Simon and Garfunkel sang in Central Park.
note: The duo's name is one organisation. Reading it as two people is defensible; this key picks the duo.

text: Marks & Spencer and Tesco cut prices.
note: & inside a name; 'and' between names.

text: She read Pride and Prejudice and Emma.
note: The first 'and' is inside a title; the second joins two titles.

text: Lennon and McCartney wrote the song.
note: Universal NER tags names joined by a conjunction separately.

text: The menu listed Coca-Cola, Sprite, and Fanta.
note: Drinks as products. Serial comma before and.

text: Liverpool beat Chelsea.
note: Football clubs, first and last word.

text: Mount Everest is tall.
note: Name starts the text.

text: The winner was Serena Williams.
note: Name ends the text before a period.

text: Oslo
note: The whole text is one name with no punctuation.

text: Thank you, Maya!
note: Sentence ! after the last name stays outside.

text: Yesterday Paul McCartney played Yesterday.
note: The first Yesterday is a time word; the last one is the song.

text: The Boeing 747 landed at Heathrow.
note: A number inside a product name.

text: Blink-182 played in Leeds.
note: Hyphen and number inside a band name.

text: He watched 2001: A Space Odyssey twice.
note: Title starts with a number and holds a colon.

text: Maroon 5 released Songs About Jane.
note: Number ends a band name.

text: She bought a PlayStation 5 in Osaka.
note: Number ends a product name.

text: In 1984 she first read 1984 by George Orwell.
note: The first 1984 is a year; the second is the novel.

text: Björk grew up in Reykjavík.
note: Accented letters; offsets count code points.

text: We ate at Café de Flore in Paris.
note: Accent and lowercase French particle.

text: Gabriel García Márquez wrote Cien años de soledad.
note: Spanish title in sentence case.

text: Łódź is a city in Poland.
note: Polish letters at the start.

text: Nestlé bought a factory in Zürich.
note: Accented company and place.

text: The team visited 東京 last year.
note: Japanese script for Tokyo.

text: The weather was cold all week.
note: No name.

text: She said it's nobody's fault.
note: Apostrophes with no name.

text: We don't know what they'll say.
note: Contractions with no name.

text: The rock 'n' roll era changed music.
note: A lowercase genre is not a name.

text: It rained on Monday and Tuesday.
note: Days are not in this label set.

text: Sir Paul McCartney played two nights in Liverpool.
note: Sir is a title and stays outside (rule 12).

text: Dr. Mae Jemison flew on the shuttle Endeavour.
note: Dr. stays outside. A named vehicle is a thing.

text: Mrs. Hudson rented the flat to Mr. Holmes.
note: Mrs. and Mr. stay outside even when only a surname follows.

text: Queen Elizabeth II opened the Sydney Opera House in 1973.
note: Queen stays outside. The regnal number stays inside (rule 13).

text: The Queen spoke on television, and the band Queen played afterwards.
note: The first Queen is a title with no name after it, so it is not a name (rule 12). The second is the band.

text: President Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address.
note: President stays outside. A named speech is a work.

text: Captain Marvel beat Captain America at the box office.
note: These are film titles here, so Captain is part of each title (rule 12 exception).

text: Dame Judi Dench and Professor Brian Cox spoke at the Royal Institution.
note: Dame and Professor stay outside. Lowercase the stays outside. An institution named as the venue of a talk is a place (rule 14); changed from organisation after the agreement study.

text: Henry VIII built the great hall at Hampton Court.
note: A regnal number is part of the name (rule 13).

text: Rocky II earned more than Rocky.
note: A sequel number is part of the title. The bare title is a separate work.

text: Louis XIV moved the court to Versailles.
note: Roman numeral inside the name.

text: She preferred Toy Story 3 to Shrek 2.
note: Arabic sequel numbers stay inside. The word 'to' between them is outside.

text: Martin Luther King III met Pope John Paul II in Rome.
note: A generational III and a regnal II stay inside. Pope is a title and stays outside.

text: Final Fantasy VII and Windows 95 both came out in the 1990s.
note: A game is a work. Software is a thing (rule 20). A decade is not a name.

text: We ate at the Williamses' house after James' party.
note: Plural family name with a bare ', and a singular name ending in s with a bare '. Both marks stay outside. A family name is a person (MUC-7 A.3.2).

text: The Bank of England's governor met the prime minister.
note: Group genitive: the 's closes the whole phrase and stays outside. The prime minister is a role, not a name.

text: Adele`s tour and Drakeʼs album sold out.
note: A backtick and a modifier-letter apostrophe (U+02BC) used as apostrophes. Any apostrophe-like mark before s is the possessive (rule 1).

text: Adele's back, and Wembley's sold out.
note: Here 's means 'is'. The contraction stays outside the name, like a possessive.

text: The court sits in The Hague.
note: A capital The in mid-sentence is part of the name (rule 14).

text: The Beatles played the Cavern Club.
note: A sentence-initial The before a name that is not a work title stays outside (rule 14). Lowercase the stays outside.

text: Tickets for The Who sold faster than tickets for the Kinks.
note: Capital The mid-sentence stays inside. Lowercase the stays outside.

text: She reads The Economist and watches The Office.
note: A magazine that is read is a work (rule 16). Capital The mid-sentence stays inside.

text: She flew from Senegal to The Gambia.
note: The country's name keeps a capital The mid-sentence.

text: A reporter at The New York Times covered the Super Bowl.
note: The paper as an employer is an organisation (rule 16). Lowercase the before Super Bowl stays outside. A sporting event is an event.

text: Washington imposed new tariffs, and Downing Street said nothing.
note: A capital and a government address stand for governments, so both are organisations (rule 16, ACE 6.1).

text: The Kremlin denied the report.
note: A government seat standing for the government. Sentence-initial The stays outside.

text: Brazil beat Argentina in the final, then flew home to Brazil.
note: Countries as teams are organisations. The last Brazil is the country.

text: Hollywood loves sequels, but Wall Street hates risk.
note: A place name standing for a whole industry keeps its literal label, place (rule 16).

text: The White House is white, and the White House vetoed the bill.
note: The building is a place. The White House that vetoes is an organisation.

text: She has read all of Dickens and owns a small Hockney.
note: A person's name standing for their works keeps the person label (rule 16). Universal NER would leave 'a Hockney' untagged.

text: Jordan scored forty points on a trip to Jordan.
note: Same spelling, a person then a country. Context decides (rule 17).

text: Amazon shipped the book up the Amazon.
note: A company then a river.

text: Paris Hilton stayed at the Paris Hilton.
note: A person then a hotel. A hotel is a place.

text: Lincoln drove a Lincoln to Lincoln.
note: A person, a car and a city, all spelled alike.

text: Mercury orbits closer to the Sun than Venus, said Freddie Mercury's biographer.
note: Planets and the Sun are places (Universal NER, MUC-7). The singer's surname is also a planet.

text: Theresa May resigned in May, and Brian May played guitar.
note: The month is not a name (rule 22). The surnames are.

text: She sold her iPad on eBay and bought adidas trainers.
note: Names keep their own case. A brand on goods is a thing; the company as a business is an organisation (rule 18).

text: The easyJet flight carried a PlayStation and a MacBook Air.
note: Lowercase-first airline. A product name that holds the maker's brand is one thing name.

text: YouTube bought ads on LinkedIn for its iOS app.
note: Capitals in mid-word. Software is a thing.

text: He typed the essay in WordPerfect on a ThinkPad.
note: Joined capitals in product names.

text: The café at IKEA sells köttbullar and Daim bars.
note: All-caps company. The Swedish common noun köttbullar is not a name. Daim is a brand of sweet, so a thing.

text: Thanks @NASA for the launch photos!
note: The @ stays outside. The handle names an organisation (rule 19).

text: Watching #Wimbledon with @andymurray tonight.
note: The # and @ stay outside. The tournament is an event. A handle that stands for a person is a person.

text: #tbt to our trip to #Lisbon.
note: A hashtag that is not a name (#tbt, 'throwback Thursday') is not tagged.

text: Follow @bbcnews for updates on #Eurovision.
note: A lowercase handle for an organisation, and an event hashtag.

text: @taylorswift13 thanked everyone. #blessed
note: A handle with digits used in place of a name. #blessed is not a name.

text: The European Space Agency (ESA) launched a probe to Jupiter.
note: The long form and the short form are two names with one label. Brackets stay outside (rule 21).

text: The Premier League [EPL] fined Chelsea.
note: Square brackets. Sentence-initial The stays outside.

text: Our lawyer cited the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in court.
note: A law and its short form, both with the extra label law.

text: MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) hired her.
note: Short form first, long form in brackets. A place inside the long form gets no second tag.

text: North and South Korea marched together at the Olympics.
note: The conjuncts share an elided head, so the whole phrase is one name (rule 23, MUC-7 4.1.1).

text: Mr. and Mrs. Smith moved to Leeds.
note: Titles stay outside, so the shared surname is the only name. It stands for two people.

text: She watched Mr. & Mrs. Smith on a flight to Rome.
note: The same words as a film title are one work, titles included.

text: Venus and Serena Williams played doubles in Paris.
note: Two first names share one surname, so the phrase is one name. Universal NER would split it into Venus and Serena Williams.

text: The Victoria and Albert Museum sits near Hyde Park.
note: The and is inside one name. A museum as a building is a place.

text:
The band opened for Pink
Floyd at Earls Court.
note: A line break inside a name stays inside (rule 24).

text:
Headliners:
Blur
Oasis
Pulp
note: Names on separate lines of a list are separate names.

text:
We toured the Rijks-
museum in Amsterdam.
note: A hyphen added at a line wrap and the break after it stay inside the name.

text: Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson filmed in Hawaii.
note: A quoted nickname inside a person's name stays inside with its quotes (rule 25, MUC-7 A.1.6.1).

text: The Fab Four landed in the Big Apple in 1964.
note: Nicknames are names with the label of what they name. Lowercase the and sentence-initial The stay outside.

text: Satchmo recorded What a Wonderful World.
note: A one-word nickname for a person, then a song title.

text: Fans call Manchester United the Red Devils.
note: A club and its nickname are both organisations.

text: Kubrick made Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb in 1964.
note: The whole title is one work, with its colon and the title word Dr.

text: Mark Haddon wrote The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time.
note: Long title with small words and a hyphen, ending the sentence.

text: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was published by Bloomsbury.
note: A character's name inside a title gets no second tag. The middle 's stays inside.

text: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford stars Brad Pitt.
note: A sentence-initial The that starts a work title stays inside. Two people named inside the title get no tags.

text: Email tickets@glastonbury.example for refunds.
note: An email address used as an address is not a name, and names inside it are not tagged (rule 26).

text: Read the review at www.rollingstone.com/music/radiohead today.
note: A web address is not a name, even with a band inside it.

text: Rolling Stone reviewed OK Computer at rollingstone.com.
note: The magazine that reviews is an organisation. The web address is not a name.

text: press@bbc.co.uk confirmed the story to Reuters.
note: An email address that acts in place of a name is tagged whole (Universal NER 2.3.10).

text: The concert on 14 July drew 20,000 fans to Lyon.
note: A date and a count are not names (rule 22).

text: Tickets cost £45 in 2019, up 12% from the 1990s.
note: Money, a year, a percentage and a decade. No names.

text: They held a Christmas party on 25 December.
note: A named holiday is an event. A plain date is not a name.

text: Studio 54 opened in April 1977 on West 54th Street.
note: Numbers inside names stay inside. The month and year are not names.

text: 🎸 Hendrix 🎸 played Woodstock
note: Emoji stay outside. The festival is an event. No final punctuation.

text: Loved Lisbon❤️ and Porto🍷!
note: Emoji touch the names. The heart is two code points, a heart and a variation selector.

text: Messi⚽️scored again for Inter Miami.
note: An emoji with no spaces between a name and the next word.

text: 👩‍🚀 Sally Ride flew on Challenger.
note: A three-code-point emoji joined by a zero-width joiner comes first. The shuttle is a thing.

text: omg saw coldplay at wembley last nite
note: Lowercase names in informal text are names (rule 11).

text: anyone else think taylor swift's new album beats folklore??
note: Lowercase possessive and an album whose real title is lowercase.

text: grabbing a starbucks b4 the arsenal game lol
note: A starbucks here is a drink, so a thing (rule 18). The club is an organisation.

text: cant believe spurs lost to villa again
note: Short club names in lower case. Both are organisations.

text: Beijing was once written Peking in English.
note: Two romanised spellings of one city are both names. A language gets the extra label language.

text: Rachmaninoff, often written Rachmaninov, left Moscow, spelled Moskva in Russian.
note: Spelling variants each count as a name (rule 27).

text: Ibn Battuta left Tangier for Mecca.
note: Arabic name particle Ibn stays inside.

text: Dostoevsky wrote Prestuplenie i nakazanie, known in English as Crime and Punishment.
note: A romanised title in sentence case, then its English title.

text: The Beatles won a Grammy Award, and Radiohead won the Mercury Prize.
note: Awards get the extra label award.

text: The Magna Carta was sealed at Runnymede in 1215.
note: A named document made into law gets the extra label law (OntoNotes LAW).

text: Parliament passed the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
note: The year and the internal comma are part of the law's name.

text: She speaks Welsh at home and Spanish at work.
note: Languages get the extra label language.

text: The French chef and the Japanese sushi master met in Lyon.
note: Nationality words, even as adjectives, get the extra label nationality (OntoNotes NORP).

text: The Battle of Hastings came long before the 2012 Summer Olympics in London.
note: Named battles and games are events. The year is inside the games' name.

text: Tesla unveiled the Model S at the Detroit Auto Show.
note: A product is a thing. A trade show is an event, and its place word gets no second tag.

text: Marie Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903.
note: The whole prize name is one award.

text: Esperanto speakers met at the World Cup in Qatar.
note: A constructed language, a tournament and a country.

text: The singer thanked the band and the prime minister.
note: Descriptions of people are not names (rule 28).

text: Adele said she wrote it herself.
note: Pronouns that refer back to a name are not names.

text: The author of Emma lived in Bath.
note: 'The author of Emma' describes a person. Only Emma and Bath are names.

text: Our president visited the mayor of Leeds.
note: Roles are not names. The place inside a role phrase is still a name.

text: They said the King would visit the city.
note: A capitalised title with no name after it is not a name (rule 12).
